Dear Mr Griffiths,

I am writing to share my views on the proposed changes to the school uniform policy.

While I understand the school values a smart, consistent appearance, I believe the current policy places an unfair financial burden on families. The branded blazer costs sixty-five pounds from the single approved supplier. Many families in this area cannot afford that, particularly when children outgrow their uniform within a year.

I am not suggesting we abandon uniform entirely. I am suggesting we allow plain alternatives that meet the same dress code without the branded logo. This would maintain standards while respecting the reality of family budgets.

I would be grateful for the opportunity to discuss this further.

Yours sincerely,
Harri Bevan
passages.label: Model A — Letter to a headteacher about school uniform

passages.text:
The Two-Hour Rule Nobody Follows

Health experts recommend no more than two hours of recreational screen time per day for teenagers. The average teenager in the UK spends seven. That is not a gap — it is a canyon.

Before you close this page (on a screen, obviously), consider what those five extra hours actually look like. They are the hour you spend watching videos you did not choose, served up by an algorithm that knows your weaknesses better than you do. They are the forty-five minutes scrolling through posts that make you feel worse about yourself. They are the two hours of gaming that were supposed to be thirty minutes.

Nobody is going to take your phone away. That ship has sailed. But knowing where those hours go is the first step to deciding whether you actually want to spend them there. Because five hours a day is thirty-five hours a week. That is almost a full-time job — and you are not getting paid.
passages.label: Model B — Article for a school magazine about screen time

passages.text:
Good evening, councillors.

I grew up on this high street. My first job was in the bakery that closed last year. My grandmother bought her wedding dress from a shop that is now a betting office. I am not here to be sentimental. I am here because the draft regeneration plan for this town centre makes the same mistake every regeneration plan makes: it asks what businesses want to move in, instead of asking what the people who live here actually need.

The plan proposes thirty-two new residential units, a gym, and a coffee chain. It does not propose a single community space. Not a youth club. Not a library. Not even a bench that is not designed to stop people sleeping on it.

I have spoken to sixty residents in the past three weeks. Do you know what they asked for? A GP surgery that is less than forty minutes away by bus. A playground that is not padlocked. A place where elderly people can sit down without buying a four-pound coffee.

Regeneration should not mean replacement. It should mean repair. And repair starts with listening to the people who never left.
passages.label: Model C — Speech to a town council about regeneration

passages.text:
Dear Mrs Jenkins,

I am writing to urge you to reconsider the proposal to cut the school's arts budget by forty per cent.

The arts are not a luxury. They are the subject where students who struggle in every other classroom suddenly excel. They are where a quiet student discovers they can command a stage. They are where a child who cannot sit still for an hour of maths focuses for three hours on a sculpture without looking up.

Last year, fourteen students chose art, drama, or music as a GCSE option. This year, the number has dropped to six. That is not a natural decline — it is the result of students hearing, term after term, that the arts do not matter. If we cut the budget again, we are not just reducing funding. We are sending a message: that creativity has no value here.

I am asking for the budget to be maintained at its current level — not increased, not ring-fenced, simply not cut. That is a modest request for a subject that shapes who our students become.

Yours sincerely,
Megan Parry

passages.text:
You Cannot Revise on Crisps and Energy Drinks

Here is a fact that no revision guide will tell you: what you eat affects how you think. A 2023 study from King's College London found that students who ate a balanced breakfast scored fifteen per cent higher in afternoon concentration tests than those who skipped it or grabbed a cereal bar on the way out.

This is not a lecture about five-a-day. This is about your grades.

The problem is not that teenagers do not know what healthy food looks like. The problem is that nobody has taught them how to make it. Cooking is not on the timetable. Parents are busy. And a microwave meal costs two pounds and takes four minutes — which, when you are revising at nine o'clock at night, feels like a perfectly rational choice.

But rational is not the same as good. A plate of scrambled eggs on toast takes six minutes, costs less, and gives your brain protein it can actually use. You do not need a recipe book. You need a frying pan and five minutes of effort.

So here is my challenge: cook one meal from scratch this week. Just one. See if you notice the difference. I think you will.

passages.text:
Good evening.

I have a question for the members of this council. When you close a library, where do you expect people to go?

The retired teacher who comes here every Tuesday to read the paper because she cannot afford a subscription. The single father who brings his daughter every Saturday because their flat has no books and no space for them. The sixteen-year-old who sits in the corner every evening because this is the only warm, quiet, free place in this town where she can revise.

Where do they go?

You will say the answer is online. You will say there are e-books and digital archives and virtual reading groups. And you will be right — those things exist. But they require a device, a broadband connection, and the confidence to use them. A third of the people who use this library do not have reliable internet at home. You know this. It is in the consultation report you commissioned.

Closing this library will save this council ninety-two thousand pounds a year. Keeping it open costs each council taxpayer roughly six pence per week. Six pence. That is less than a single sheet of the paper this report was printed on.

So when you vote tonight, I ask you to remember this: a library is not a cost. It is the cheapest, most democratic institution this country has ever invented. Do not close it because you have forgotten what it is for.
passages.label: Model C — Speech persuading a council to save a library

Homework Does Not Work. Here Is Why.

Every evening, millions of students sit at kitchen tables completing worksheets that will be glanced at, ticked, and never looked at again. This is not education. It is administration.

The evidence against homework is stronger than most teachers realise. A 2015 study by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development found no consistent link between the amount of homework assigned and academic achievement at secondary level. Finland — routinely the highest-performing education system in Europe — assigns less homework than almost any other country. The pattern is clear: more homework does not mean more learning.

The counterargument is that homework teaches discipline. Perhaps. But it also teaches something else: that learning is a chore to be endured after the real day is over. A student who reads for pleasure, plays a sport, or builds something in their spare time is learning more than one who copies answers from a friend on the bus.

Homework is not sacred. It is a habit. And habits should be questioned.

passages.text:
Dear Editor,

The proposal to enforce a minimum age of sixteen for social media accounts has been dismissed by many as unworkable. They are wrong.

The current system relies on self-declaration: a thirteen-year-old ticks a box saying they are old enough, and the platform accepts it. This is not regulation. It is a formality that exists so companies can say they tried while continuing to profit from users whose brains are still developing.

Critics argue that enforcement is impossible — that teenagers will simply lie about their age. But this argument proves too much. We do not abandon speed limits because some drivers break them. We do not stop selling alcohol to under-eighteens because fake IDs exist. The point of a law is not to prevent every violation. It is to create a standard, and to make violation something that requires effort rather than a single click.

The evidence of harm is no longer debatable. Internal documents from the platforms themselves — leaked in 2021 — show that their own researchers found links between teenage use and increased rates of anxiety, depression, and body dissatisfaction. The companies knew. They did nothing. The law should do what they would not.

Yours faithfully,
Rhys Morgan

Good morning — though I suspect, for most of you, it does not feel very good at all.

I want to make an argument that is supported by decades of research, endorsed by the American Academy of Pediatrics, and ignored by almost every school in this country: that secondary schools should start no earlier than nine-thirty.

The science is simple. During adolescence, the brain's internal clock shifts forward by approximately two hours. A teenager told to sleep at ten and wake at seven is biologically equivalent to an adult told to sleep at eight and wake at five. You would not function well on that schedule. Neither do they.

The objection I hear most often is logistics. Parents need to get to work. Buses run on fixed timetables. After-school clubs would finish too late. These are real problems. I am not pretending they are trivial. But they are organisational problems — and organisational problems can be solved. The sleep deprivation we are imposing on teenagers cannot be solved by willpower or an earlier bedtime. It is biological.

A 2017 trial in Seattle moved school start times from seven-fifty to eight-forty-five. Attendance improved. Grades improved. Chronic lateness fell by one third. The students did not just feel better — they performed better. And the logistics worked themselves out within a term.

We have built an education system around adult convenience and called it tradition. I am asking us to build it around the students instead.

passages.text:
How to Survive Exam Season Without Losing Your Mind

If you are reading this, you are probably already stressed. That is normal. In fact, it would be strange if you were not. Exams matter, and caring about them is not a weakness — it is a sign that you take your future seriously.

But there is a difference between healthy pressure and the kind of stress that stops you sleeping, eating, or thinking clearly. If you have crossed that line, here are three things that might help.

First, break your revision into small, timed blocks. Thirty minutes on one topic, then a ten-minute break. Your brain retains more from six short sessions than from one six-hour marathon.

Second, talk to someone. Not about revision — about how you feel. A parent, a friend, a teacher. Stress shrinks when you say it out loud.

Third, move. Walk, run, stretch, dance in your room — it does not matter what. Exercise releases chemicals that reduce anxiety. You do not need a gym membership. You need fifteen minutes and a pair of trainers.

You will get through this. Thousands of students do, every single year. You are not the exception.

passages.text:
Hi Sam,

I know you are stressing about options, and I get it — it feels like you are making decisions that will define the rest of your life. But here is the thing: you are not. Options matter, but they do not lock you into anything permanent.

Here is what I wish someone had told me. Pick at least one subject you genuinely enjoy, even if it is not the most 'useful' on paper. You are going to spend two years studying it. If you hate every lesson, your grades will suffer regardless of how strategic the choice looked in Year 9.

If you are torn between two subjects, ask yourself this: which one do I want to learn about even when no one is testing me? That is usually the right answer.

Avoid choosing a subject just because your friends are doing it. I did that with geography. I do not regret many things, but I regret that. You will make new friends in any class — and you will enjoy the subject more if you actually chose it for yourself.

Finally, talk to the teachers. Not to ask 'what should I pick?' — they cannot answer that. Ask them what the course actually involves. The Year 9 taster is not always representative.

You have got this. Whatever you pick, you will make it work.

From,
Alex

passages.text:
When the Group Chat Turns Against You

It starts small. A message you were not meant to see. A screenshot shared without context. A joke at your expense that everyone laughs at except you. And suddenly, the group chat — the place where you arrange plans and share memes — feels like a courtroom where you are the only one on trial.

If this sounds familiar, here is the first thing to know: you are not overreacting. Online conflict feels disproportionately painful because it is public, permanent, and happening in a space you cannot leave without feeling like you have lost. That combination is designed to make you feel powerless. Understanding that is the first step to taking back control.

Do not reply immediately. This is the hardest advice to follow and the most important. Every message sent in anger becomes evidence that will be screenshot and shared. Give yourself twenty minutes. If you still want to reply after that, write it in your notes app first. Read it back. Then decide.

If the conflict involves someone spreading lies or targeting you repeatedly, that is not drama — it is bullying. And bullying requires adult intervention, not a cleverer comeback. Tell a teacher, a parent, or a trusted adult. You are not being weak. You are being strategic.

Finally, remember that a group chat is not a jury. The people laughing along are not all against you — most of them are just relieved it is not happening to them. That does not make it acceptable. But it does mean you have more allies than you think.

You will survive this. The chat will move on. You need to make sure you do too — without carrying it with you.

passages.text:
Forty Minutes, One Hatch, Six Hundred Students

Every lunchtime, the same thing happens. The bell rings. Six hundred students funnel towards a single serving hatch. By the time most of us reach the front, half our lunch break is gone. What arrives on the tray is lukewarm pasta or a sandwich that has been sitting in cling film since seven o'clock that morning.

This is not a complaint about the kitchen staff, who work hard with limited resources. It is a complaint about the system. One hatch for six hundred students is a design problem, not a staffing one. Other schools in the area have introduced pre-order apps that cut queue times in half. Ours has not considered it.

If the school is serious about student wellbeing — and the posters on every corridor wall suggest it is — then it should start with the meal that fuels the entire afternoon.

passages.text:
The Invisible Workforce Propping Up This Town

Every Saturday morning, before most adults in this town have finished their coffee, thirty-two teenagers are already at work. They are not being paid. They are not doing it for a Duke of Edinburgh certificate. They are doing it because the food bank on Station Road cannot operate without them.

Last year, the Station Road Food Bank distributed twelve thousand meals. Seven thousand of those were packed, sorted, and delivered by volunteers under the age of eighteen. That is not a footnote — it is the entire operation. Without those young hands, the shelves would be empty by Tuesday.

We hear a great deal about what is wrong with young people. We hear about screen addiction, antisocial behaviour, and falling standards. What we hear far less about is the sixteen-year-old who gives up every Saturday morning to make sure a stranger's child does not go to bed hungry.

This article is not asking for donations — the food bank has enough tins. It is asking for something harder: that the next time you read a headline about lazy teenagers, you remember the ones who were up before you, doing work you would not do for free.

passages.text:
We Did Not Kill the High Street. We Just Stopped Noticing It Was Dying.

The last independent bookshop in this town closed on Friday. It did not make the local news. Nobody protested. A handful of people posted about it online, tagged their friends, and moved on. By Monday, the shutters were down and the landlord was advertising the unit as available for a vape shop or a betting office — the only businesses, it seems, that can still afford the rent.

We will be told this is inevitable. That online shopping killed the high street. That people voted with their wallets and the market responded. This is partially true — but only partially. What also killed the high street was parking charges that punish anyone who stays longer than forty-five minutes. It was business rates that charge a small bakery the same per square metre as a chain pharmacy. It was a council that spent two million pounds on decorative planters and zero on rent relief.

The high street is not dead because people stopped wanting it. It is dead because the people who could have saved it decided that market forces were an acceptable eulogy.

There is still time. But not much. And not if we keep doing what we have always done: noticing the shutters, sighing, and walking to the retail park.

Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to express my concern about the recent changes to the number 42 bus service, which has been reduced from every twenty minutes to every forty-five.

This route is the only public transport connection between Llanberis and the nearest secondary school. Over three hundred students rely on it every morning. Since the timetable change, students have been arriving late to registration, missing first period, or being forced to stand in the rain at stops with no shelter for up to forty minutes.

I understand that bus companies must operate within financial constraints. However, cutting a service that is the sole transport option for school-age children is not an efficiency saving. It is a failure of responsibility.

I would be grateful if you could review this decision and consider reinstating the twenty-minute frequency during term-time mornings.

Yours faithfully,
Seren Davies

Dear Ms Carter,

I am writing on behalf of the Year 10 geography group to propose a field trip to the Brecon Beacons National Park as part of our controlled assessment preparation.

The controlled assessment requires primary data collection on river processes. Currently, our preparation has been limited to textbook diagrams and classroom simulations, which — while useful — cannot replicate the experience of measuring flow velocity, channel width, and sediment size at a real river site. The Afon Mellte offers an accessible and well-documented study location that has been used by several schools in the region.

I am aware that residential trips carry significant cost. To address this, we have costed a single-day visit using the school minibus, reducing the expense to approximately eight pounds per student for fuel and packed lunch contributions. We have also identified three parent volunteers willing to assist with supervision.

The trip would directly improve the quality of our controlled assessments by providing authentic data. I believe this represents excellent value for the educational benefit it would deliver.

I would welcome the opportunity to present this proposal in more detail at your convenience.

Yours sincerely,
Owen Hughes

Dear Editor,

I write in response to last week's article celebrating the planning approval for two hundred and forty new homes on the Cwmbach meadow site. The article described the development as 'a much-needed boost for the local economy.' I would like to offer a different perspective.

The Cwmbach meadow is the last remaining green space between the town centre and the river. It is where families walk their dogs. It is where children from the estate next door play after school, because the nearest playground is a twenty-minute walk across a dual carriageway. It is where flood water collects harmlessly during heavy rain — a function that two hundred and forty homes and a car park will not replicate.

The developer's environmental impact assessment acknowledges, on page forty-seven, that the site sits in a flood risk zone. It proposes a drainage system designed to handle a once-in-thirty-year flooding event. What it does not mention is that this area has flooded three times in the last five years. A once-in-thirty-year design is not caution. It is wishful thinking.

I am not opposed to new housing. This town needs it. But building on the one site that serves simultaneously as a public amenity, a wildlife habitat, and a natural flood defence is not solving a housing crisis. It is creating three new ones.

I urge your readers — and the council — to attend the public consultation on Thursday and demand that this decision is revisited before the first digger arrives.

Yours faithfully,
Anwen Rhys

passages.text:
A School Play That Forgot It Was Supposed to Be Amateur

I went to the Year 11 production of Blood Brothers expecting the usual: missed cues, wobbly scenery, and that one student who shouts every line because they think volume equals emotion. What I got was something entirely different.

From the opening number, it was clear that this cast had rehearsed beyond the point of competence and into the territory of actual performance. Lily Tran, as Mrs Johnstone, carried the first act almost single-handedly. Her voice cracked on 'Tell Me It's Not True' — not from nerves, but from a deliberate, controlled fragility that made the audience hold their breath.

The set was simple: a raised platform, two chairs, a streetlamp. It worked because the lighting did the heavy lifting. Director Mr Ahmed used shadow and colour to shift between the Johnstone kitchen and the Lyons household without a single scene change. Clever, efficient, and visually striking.

It was not perfect. The second act dragged in places, and the gunshot sound effect was so quiet it got a laugh instead of a gasp. But these are minor complaints about a production that punched well above its weight.

Go next year. Whatever they do, it will be worth your evening.

passages.text:
Nain's Kitchen: Where the Food Is Excellent and the Chairs Are Not

Nain's Kitchen opened three months ago on the high street, in the unit that has been, at various points, a phone repair shop, a nail bar, and an optimistic attempt at a juice bar. The decor suggests it is still deciding what it wants to be. The chairs are mismatched. The menu is written in chalk on a board that has clearly been wiped and rewritten several times. The lighting is the kind that makes everyone look slightly ill.

None of this matters, because the food is extraordinary.

The lamb cawl arrived in a bowl the size of a small planet, thick with root vegetables and scattered with fresh parsley. It tasted like something a grandmother would make if that grandmother had trained at a Michelin-starred restaurant and then decided she preferred feeding people for seven pounds a bowl. The bara brith came warm, with salted butter that melted on contact.

Service was slow. Not rudely slow — more the pace of a place that is genuinely cooking everything from scratch and has not yet worked out how to do that for thirty covers at once. I waited twenty minutes for a main course. I did not mind, because when it arrived, it was worth forty.

Nain's Kitchen is not polished. It is not Instagram-ready. But it is honest, delicious, and seven pounds for a bowl of cawl that could feed two. Go before the secret gets out.

passages.text:
How to Be Sixteen: The Film That Finally Gets It Right

There is a particular kind of teenage film that adults love: one where the protagonist learns an important lesson, hugs their parent, and walks into the sunset a better person. How to Be Sixteen is not that film. Thank God.

Director Nia Evans has made a film about being sixteen that feels like actually being sixteen: boring in stretches, confusing in the middle, and punctuated by moments of such acute embarrassment that I had to look away from the screen.

The plot is thin by design. Ffion, played with devastating understatement by newcomer Megan Lloyd, spends a summer in a small Welsh town waiting for something to happen. She argues with her mother. She develops a crush that goes nowhere. She gets a job at a caravan park and quits after three days. Nothing dramatic occurs. And that is precisely the point.

Evans understands something that most teen films do not: that the defining experience of adolescence is not a single transformative event. It is the slow, uncomfortable realisation that you are becoming someone, and you have no idea who. Ffion does not grow up by the end credits. She just grows slightly. And that feels more honest than a hundred coming-of-age speeches.

The film is not without flaws. The subplot about Ffion's father is underdeveloped, and the soundtrack — heavy on Welsh indie bands — occasionally overwhelms the quieter scenes. But these are the scratches on an otherwise remarkable debut.

If you are sixteen, this film will make you feel seen. If you are no longer sixteen, it will make you remember. Either way, it is two hours well spent.

I want to ask you a question, and I want you to answer honestly — not out loud, just in your head. How many mornings this week have you spent even thirty seconds thinking about what to wear to school?

None. That is the answer for most of you, and that is exactly the point.

School uniform removes a decision that nobody needs to make. It removes the pressure to keep up, the quiet judgement of who can afford what, the daily reminder that some families have more money than others. Uniform does not make everyone equal — nothing can do that — but it removes one visible way in which inequality walks through the school gates every morning.

I know what some of you are thinking. You want to express yourselves. You want to be individuals. And I respect that — genuinely. But individuality is not a shirt. It is not a pair of trainers. It is what you say, what you think, what you create, and how you treat people. Those things cannot be bought, and they cannot be taken away by a dress code.

passages.text:
Good evening. Thank you for coming.

I know why most of you are here. You are worried about screens. You are worried about the hours your children spend staring at phones, at tablets, at laptops — and you want someone to tell you what to do about it. I understand that worry. I share it.

But I am not going to stand here and tell you to ban screens. That would be dishonest, because it would not work, and it would be patronising, because you already know it would not work. Your children live in a digital world. They do their homework on screens. They talk to their friends on screens. They read the news — when they read the news — on screens. Removing the screen would be like removing the telephone in 1985: technically possible, practically absurd.

What I am going to suggest is something harder than a ban. I am going to suggest a conversation. Not a lecture, not a set of rules pinned to the fridge, but an honest conversation about what screens give us and what they take away. Because your children are not stupid. They know that scrolling for two hours does not make them happy. They just do not know what else to do with the silence.

The real question is not how much screen time is too much. The real question is: what are we offering instead?
passages.label: Model B — Speech to parents on screen time

passages.text:
Councillor Davies. Members of the panel. Residents.

Three weeks ago, I watched a group of fourteen-year-olds spend their Saturday morning picking litter from the canal path behind Westfield Road. They filled nine bags. Nobody asked them to do it. Nobody paid them. Nobody filmed it for social media. They did it because their town looked neglected, and they decided it should not.

I mention this not because it is remarkable, but because it is not. Young people in this town volunteer every week — at the food bank, at the community garden, at the sheltered housing on Priory Lane. They do it quietly, consistently, and without recognition. And yet when this council discusses youth provision, the conversation always begins with the same word: problems. Youth crime. Youth unemployment. Youth antisocial behaviour. As if the only thing young people produce is trouble.

I am here to ask you to change the first word. Not from problems to solutions — that is too neat, too motivational-poster. I am asking you to change it to investment. Because when a fourteen-year-old fills nine bags of litter on a Saturday morning, that is not volunteering. That is a young person investing in a place that has not yet invested in them.

Fund the youth centre. Reopen the Saturday programme. Match every hour a young person gives with a pound towards training, transport, or equipment. Not because they have earned it — they have earned it ten times over — but because it is the intelligent thing to do. A town that ignores its young volunteers does not save money. It spends it later, on problems that need not have existed.

Dear Councillor Marchetti,

I am writing to express my concern about the proposed closure of Riverside Park as part of the council's cost-saving review. While I understand the financial pressures the council faces, I believe this decision would cause significant harm to the community it is intended to serve.

Riverside Park is not a luxury. It is the only green space within walking distance for over three thousand residents, many of whom are elderly or do not have access to a car. For these residents, the park is not a pleasant addition to their week — it is the only place they can walk safely, sit outdoors, and see another person. Closing it does not save money. It transfers the cost to the NHS, which will bear the burden of increased isolation, inactivity, and deteriorating mental health.

I would welcome the opportunity to discuss alternative savings that do not remove a public resource from the people who need it most.

Yours sincerely,
Olivia Rendall

Let me be honest with you: nobody is going to read this and suddenly start eating salad for breakfast. That is not what this is about.

Healthy eating is not about being perfect. It is not about cutting out everything you enjoy and replacing it with something that tastes like disappointment. It is about knowing what your body actually needs and giving it a fighting chance.

Here is the truth that the wellness influencers will not tell you: you do not need to spend forty pounds on a smoothie maker. You do not need to buy organic avocados or chia seeds or whatever the internet has decided is essential this week. You need water. You need fruit. You need something with protein that is not a packet of crisps at 2pm because you skipped lunch again.

The problem is not that you do not know what healthy food looks like. You have had that lesson a hundred times. The problem is that healthy food is often more expensive, less convenient, and less available than the cheap stuff. Until that changes, telling teenagers to eat better is just noise.

So no, I am not going to lecture you. But I am going to say this: drink some water. Eat something before midday. And stop pretending that three energy drinks count as breakfast.

passages.text:
There is a particular cruelty in cutting the arts from schools and then blaming young people for lacking creativity. It is like removing the ladder and criticising them for not reaching the shelf.

Across the country, music rooms are being converted into storage. Drama studios are being repurposed as exam halls. Art departments that once employed three teachers now survive on one, plus a teaching assistant who doubles as the person who orders the paint. These are not the casualties of declining interest. They are the casualties of a funding model that measures education in spreadsheets and has never found a column for joy.

The argument against arts funding is always the same: it is not economically productive. It does not lead to secure employment. It does not contribute to GDP in the way that engineering or finance does. And there is a version of this argument that is defensible — resources are limited, and choices must be made.

But the argument is built on a false premise. The creative industries contribute over a hundred billion pounds to the UK economy each year. Film, music, design, advertising, gaming — these are not hobbies. They are industries, and they need trained people. Every school that closes its art department is closing a pipeline to one of the fastest-growing sectors in the country.

The deeper problem, though, is not economic. It is human. Art teaches young people to express what they cannot say, to process what they do not yet understand, and to see the world through someone else's eyes. Remove that, and you do not just lose an industry. You lose a generation that knows how to think but has forgotten how to feel.

passages.text:
Every morning, thousands of teenagers drag themselves out of bed at six-thirty. They eat breakfast — if they eat breakfast — with their eyes half closed. They arrive at school tired, irritable, and unable to concentrate on anything before ten o'clock. And then we wonder why results are not improving.

The science is not new. Adolescent circadian rhythms shift during puberty, meaning teenagers naturally fall asleep later and wake later. Asking a fifteen-year-old to be alert at eight-thirty is like asking an adult to be sharp at four in the morning. It is not laziness. It is biology.

The obvious objection is logistics. Parents need to get to work. Buses run on fixed timetables. After-school clubs would finish later. These are real concerns, and they deserve honest answers — not dismissal, but not the power to shut down the conversation either.

Schools in parts of Scandinavia and the United States have already made the change. Results improved. Attendance improved. Mental health improved. The evidence does not suggest that later start times might help. It suggests that earlier start times are actively harmful.

The question is not whether this is a good idea. The question is how long we are willing to keep ignoring the evidence because changing the timetable feels inconvenient.

passages.text:
Dear Editor,

I read your article about library closures with a frustration I suspect many of your readers share. The argument — that libraries are an outdated luxury in the age of the internet — is one I hear often, and it is wrong in a way that matters.

A library is not a building full of books. It is a building full of access. Access to warmth, for the homeless man who sits in the reference section every morning because there is nowhere else to go. Access to Wi-Fi, for the student whose family cannot afford broadband. Access to help, for the elderly woman who needs someone to show her how to apply for her pension online because the government has decided that everything must now be digital.

Those who argue that the internet has made libraries obsolete are making an assumption so basic it barely qualifies as thought: they are assuming that everyone has the internet. They are assuming that everyone has a quiet room, a working laptop, and the digital literacy to navigate a world that changes its interface every six months.

Closing a library does not move its users online. It moves them nowhere.

The cost of keeping a local library open is approximately fifty thousand pounds a year. The cost of the social problems that follow its closure — isolation, digital exclusion, lost learning — is incalculable. If we cannot afford fifty thousand pounds to keep a community connected, we are not making a financial decision. We are making a moral one.

Yours faithfully,
Daniel Osei

passages.text:
The debate about social media regulation tends to polarise quickly. On one side: concerned parents and politicians calling for bans, age limits, and government intervention. On the other: technology companies and libertarians insisting that regulation stifles innovation and that personal responsibility should be enough. Both positions contain truth. Neither is sufficient.

The case for regulation begins with a simple observation: social media companies do not sell a product. They sell attention. Their platforms are designed — deliberately, precisely, and at enormous expense — to keep users scrolling. The infinite feed, the autoplay, the notification that arrives at exactly the moment you were about to put the phone down: these are not accidents. They are engineering decisions, and they are optimised for engagement, not wellbeing.

This matters because the users most affected are the ones least equipped to resist. A thirty-five-year-old with a stable career and a mortgage might scroll for twenty minutes and put the phone away. A thirteen-year-old whose social world exists entirely online does not have that luxury. The platform is designed to hold them, and it does.

The case against regulation is that it is slow, blunt, and easily circumvented. Governments do not understand technology well enough to write effective laws. Companies adapt faster than legislators can respond. And there is a genuine philosophical question about where the state's right to intervene ends and individual freedom begins.

But this argument assumes that the current situation is neutral — that without regulation, people are free. They are not. They are subject to manipulation by algorithms they do not understand, designed by companies they cannot hold accountable. Regulation does not restrict freedom. It restores it.

The answer is not a ban. It is transparency. Force companies to publish how their algorithms work. Require them to offer genuinely chronological feeds alongside algorithmic ones. Make them liable when their design decisions cause measurable harm. This is not radical. It is what we already expect from food companies, pharmaceutical companies, and car manufacturers. The only reason we do not expect it from social media is that we have not yet decided to.

Young people today volunteer more than any previous generation. They staff food banks on weekends. They raise thousands for charities through sponsored events. They organise litter picks, park clean-ups, and community gardens in neighbourhoods most adults have given up on. This is not because anyone forces them. It is because they care — and because caring, for this generation, is not a slogan. It is an action.

Adults often underestimate teenagers; they assume that young people care only about screens and status. This is an unfair stereotype, and it says more about the adults than the teenagers. Most young people I know are passionate about their communities. They simply lack the platforms, the resources, and the recognition they deserve.

Volunteering builds confidence, teaches transferable skills, and introduces young people to parts of their community they might never otherwise encounter. Employers value it. Universities notice it. And more importantly, the people who benefit from it — the families fed, the parks cleared, the elderly visited — remember it long after the volunteers have moved on.

If you still believe that teenagers are lazy and self-obsessed, perhaps it is time to look more carefully at what they actually do — and to ask yourself why you have not noticed until now.

passages.text:
The dress costs four pounds. It is available in fourteen colours. It will arrive tomorrow, packaged in plastic, delivered by a driver who is not technically employed by the company that dispatched it. You will wear it once — maybe twice — and then it will join the sixty-five kilograms of clothing that the average British household throws away each year.

This is fast fashion, and it depends on a simple calculation: if the price is low enough, the buyer will not ask how. They will not ask who sewed the seams at three in the morning in a factory with no fire exits. They will not ask what happens to the dye that runs into rivers in Bangladesh. They will not ask where the dress goes when it leaves the charity bag and enters a landfill site in Ghana.

The industry's defenders argue that cheap clothing is democratic. It allows people who cannot afford designer labels to dress well, to feel confident, to participate in fashion on their own terms. This is not a trivial point; for many families, affordable clothing is a necessity, not a luxury.

But democracy built on exploitation is not democracy. It is convenience disguised as choice. The four-pound dress is cheap because someone, somewhere, is paying the real price — in wages too low to live on, in rivers too polluted to drink from, in landfill sites too vast to ignore.

The solution is not to stop buying clothes. It is to start asking questions. Where was this made? By whom? Under what conditions? And if the company cannot answer — or will not — then the price on the label is not the real price. It is just the part they are willing to show you.

passages.text:
Dear Ms Okonkwo,

I am writing to share my views on how our school should prioritise its limited budget for the coming year. This is a difficult conversation, and I appreciate that every decision means something else goes unfunded. But if I were asked to name the single most important investment, it would be mental health support.

The waiting list for counselling in this school is eight weeks long. That is eight weeks during which a student in crisis has nowhere to turn except a form tutor who — through no fault of their own — is not trained for the kind of conversations these students need. A full-time counsellor, available every day, would not solve every problem. But it would mean that no student waits two months to be heard.

I understand that the budget cannot stretch to everything. Science equipment is outdated. The library needs restocking. The sports hall roof still leaks. These are real needs, and I do not dismiss them. But a student who is struggling mentally cannot learn, cannot concentrate, and cannot benefit from any of those resources until they are well enough to walk through the door.

Thank you for reading this. I hope you will consider it.

Yours sincerely,
Kai Morgan
passages.label: Model A — Task 1: Letter to headteacher on school funding priorities

passages.text:
Nobody Talks About the Waiting List

There is a number that should bother every student in this school, and it is this: eight weeks. That is how long you wait, right now, to see the school counsellor. Eight weeks. In adult terms, that is two months. In student terms — exam terms, friendship terms, the terms in which your life actually operates — it is a lifetime.

Let me be clear about what eight weeks means. It means a student who tells a teacher they are struggling on a Monday in October will not sit down with a trained professional until December. It means that student spends eight weeks managing alone, pretending to be fine, or — and this is the outcome nobody wants to say out loud — getting worse.

This is not a criticism of the school. The counsellor we have is excellent, overworked, and doing the job of three people. The problem is not effort. It is funding. One counsellor for eleven hundred students is not a service. It is a gesture.

So what do we do? We talk about it. Not in assemblies where someone reads a PowerPoint about mindfulness, but in real conversations — honest ones — about what happens when help is not available fast enough. And we ask the people with the budget to make mental health a priority, not a poster on the wall.

Because a school that teaches resilience but cannot offer support when resilience fails is not practising what it preaches. It is hoping nobody notices.

TASK 1 — Letter to local newspaper

Dear Editor,

I read your recent article on rural depopulation with interest and — if I am honest — frustration. The argument that young people are abandoning the countryside because they are lazy or ungrateful misses the point so completely it is hard to know where to begin.

Young people leave because there is nothing to stay for. The bus runs twice a day. The nearest sixth form is twelve miles away. The GP surgery closed last year. When your options are a forty-minute drive to a minimum-wage job or a train to a city with actual opportunities, the choice is not difficult. It is not even a choice.

If we want young people to stay, we have to give them a reason to. Fund the transport. Reopen the surgery. Build the affordable housing that means a twenty-five-year-old does not need a six-figure salary to live in the village where they grew up. Until then, calling them disloyal is not just unfair. It is dishonest.

Yours faithfully,
Elena Marsh

---

TASK 2 — Article for a youth magazine

Why I Left — and Why I Might Go Back

I grew up in a village with one pub, one shop, and one bus. The pub closed when I was fourteen. The shop survived on stubbornness and lottery tickets. The bus came twice a day if you were lucky, and once if you were not.

I left for university and I did not look back. The city had everything the village did not: jobs, people, noise, things to do at nine o'clock on a Tuesday that were not staring at a field. I told myself I would never go back.

But here is the thing nobody tells you about cities: they are lonely in a way that villages are not. In the village, everybody knew me. In the city, nobody does. In the village, silence was peaceful. In the city, silence means everyone is too busy to notice you exist.

I am not romanticising the countryside. It needs better transport, better broadband, and better opportunities before anyone under thirty can realistically live there. But the thing it has — the thing cities cannot manufacture — is community. And I am starting to wonder whether I traded something valuable for something merely convenient.

statements.text: Plan both tasks before writing either one
statements.explain: Planning both tasks first means you know what each response needs. You will not accidentally use your best ideas on Task 1 and have nothing left for Task 2.

statements.explain: A slightly imperfect Task 1 plus a complete Task 2 will always score higher than a perfect Task 1 with a half-finished Task 2.

statements.explain: This feels like it saves time but usually wastes it — without a plan, you repeat ideas, lose focus, and cannot build a logical structure. Five minutes planning is an investment.

statements.explain: The exam gives two different tasks (e.g., letter then article). Matching each format shows adaptability and prevents the examiner feeling they are reading the same response twice.

passages.text:
Thank you, Mrs Henderson. And thank you to everyone who has stayed behind for this discussion — I know it is the end of the day, and I know most of you would rather be somewhere else. Which, now I think about it, is exactly my point.

The proposal on the table is that every student in this school must complete twenty hours of community service per year. On the surface, it sounds reasonable. Who could argue against volunteering? But I am not arguing against volunteering. I am arguing against compulsion — because compulsory volunteering is not volunteering at all. It is unpaid labour with a better name.

Volunteering works because it is chosen. The student who spends their Saturday at the food bank does so because they want to make a difference, not because a register is being taken. The moment you make it compulsory, you change the motivation. You turn generosity into compliance. And the people who were already volunteering — the ones who did not need to be told — now have their genuine commitment reduced to a box-ticking exercise.

I am not saying students should not be encouraged to volunteer. I am saying they should not be forced. There is a difference, and it matters.

Thank you.

passages.text:
The Case for Doing Nothing

Here is an experiment. Put your phone in another room. Not on silent — in another room, where you cannot see it, hear it, or reach it without getting up. Now sit still for ten minutes and do nothing.

If the thought of that makes you uncomfortable, you have just proved my point.

We have become a generation that cannot sit with silence. Every spare moment is filled — scrolling, swiping, watching, listening, refreshing. We check our phones within four minutes of waking up. We check them last thing at night. We check them in the bathroom, in the queue, at the traffic light, and — let us be honest — during conversations we are pretending to pay attention to.

A digital detox is not about hating technology. It is about remembering what your brain feels like when it is not being fed a constant stream of other people's opinions, achievements, and curated lives. It is about discovering that boredom — real boredom, the kind where you stare at a ceiling and think — is not something to be cured. It is something to be recovered.

You do not need to go off-grid. You do not need to delete every app or cancel every subscription. Start with one hour. One hour a day without a screen, doing something that does not require electricity: walking, reading, cooking, sitting in a garden and watching a bird do whatever birds do when they think nobody is looking.

The world will still be there when you pick the phone up again. The notifications will still be waiting. Nothing will have changed — except, perhaps, you.

TASK 1 — Letter to a Member of Parliament

Dear Ms Whitfield MP,

I am writing to urge you to support the proposed review of the GCSE examination system. I believe that the current model — two years of study assessed in a handful of three-hour exams — fails a significant proportion of students, and that a blended approach incorporating coursework, practical assessment, and examination would be fairer, more accurate, and more reflective of the skills that employers actually need.

The argument for exams is standardisation: everyone sits the same paper, on the same day, under the same conditions. I accept this. But standardisation is not the same as fairness. A system that treats every student identically does not treat every student equitably. The student with test anxiety, the student whose medication changed the week before, the student who thinks deeply but writes slowly — these are not edge cases. They are a significant minority whose abilities the current system systematically fails to measure.

I am not asking you to abolish exams. I am asking you to support a system that supplements them — so that a student's future is not determined by their worst three hours, but by their best sustained effort.

Yours sincerely,
Amara Okafor

---

TASK 2 — Blog post for students

Your Exams Do Not Define You (But the System Thinks They Do)

Let me tell you something that every teacher knows but nobody is allowed to say in an assembly: the exam system is not designed to find out what you know. It is designed to find out what you can write down in three hours under fluorescent lights while your hand cramps and the clock ticks and the person next to you sniffs every eleven seconds.

That is not intelligence. That is endurance.

I am not saying exams do not matter — they do, because the system says they do, and the system is the thing that opens doors or closes them. But there is a difference between something mattering and something being fair. Exams matter. Exams are not fair. Both of these things are true at the same time.

So what do you do? You play the game. You revise, you practise, you learn the mark schemes, and you give the examiner exactly what they are looking for. Not because the system deserves your compliance, but because your future deserves your best effort — even within a system that does not always deserve it.

And then, when you are old enough to change things, you change them.
